sections.heading: Dialogue III, Knot x, part 2 (printed pp. 353–361)
rows: [Margin, pp. 353–354: Veritatem propositionum de futuro contingenti non salvare libertatem.]
[Margin, pp. 353–354: That the truth of propositions about the contingent future does not save liberty.]

Andab. Verum tu me prorsus coepisti, video enim ad libertatis humanae cum praedefinitione divina pacem nihil ex hac sententia profici, si futuritionis ratio in causa ponatur: tunc enim actus voluntatis idcirco futurus est, quia Deus praefinivit eum futurum, & hoc originaliter; ad quod vitandum maxime haec sententia a modernis acceptatur & propugnatur.

Andab. But you have altogether caught [coepisti] me, for I see that toward the peace of human liberty with the divine predefinition [praedefinitione] nothing is advanced [profici] from this opinion [sententia], if the reason [ratio] of futurition be placed in the cause: for then the act of the will is future for this reason, because God predefined [praefinivit] it [as] future, and this originally [originaliter]; for avoiding which [thing] this opinion is accepted and defended [propugnatur] chiefly [maxime] by the moderns [modernis].

Praeterea quid de futuris conditionatis quae naturalem connexionem nullam habent, agetur? si enim a Deo pendet futuritio, & in Deo progressus est demonstrativus, & demonstratio certo itinere ad unum fertur, futura autem conditionate manifeste in deviis ab hoc itinere habitant, postquam absolute futura non sunt, clarissimum fit nullam manere eorum futuritionem. Haec tamen in cognitione divina ad moderandam libertatem humanam necessaria sunt. Considerandum itaque denuo mihi est quam viam ingrediendum sit.

Besides, what will be done about the conditioned futures [futuris conditionatis], which have no natural connexion? For if futurition depends on God, and in God the progress is demonstrative, and demonstration is borne by a certain road to one [thing], but [things] conditionally future manifestly dwell in the by-ways [deviis] from this road, since [postquam] they are not absolutely future, it becomes most clear that no futurition of them remains. These [things], however, are necessary in the divine cognition for regulating [moderandam] human liberty. It is therefore to be considered by me anew which way is to be entered [ingrediendum].

Ereu. Ego vero Massinissae invidere desisto hodie, qui, si recte memini, in Africam ad Scipionem illum Africanum maiorem profectus, ingenti illi ipsius contra Hannibalem praelio spectator affuit (ut ille canit) sua sine parte pericli; in quo neque fortuna, neque scientia ulli parti defuit, sola autem militum fortitudo orbis terrarum Imperium decidit.

Ereu. I for my part cease today to envy Massinissa, who, if I remember rightly, having set out into Africa to that Scipio Africanus the elder, was present as a spectator at that huge battle of his against Hannibal (as that [poet] sings) without his own share of the danger [sua sine parte pericli]; in which neither fortune nor science [scientia] was lacking to any [ulli] party, but the fortitude of the soldiers alone decided the Empire of the orb of the lands.

Quod enim sibi invicem Duces praestiterunt praeconium, non potuisse per artem militarem acies certius instrui: hanc ergo utrique vestrum in hoc incruento praelio laudem debitam fero: neque subtilius proponi neque acutius vitari ullo modo argumentum potuisse.

For the proclamation [praeconium] which the Generals rendered to each other in turn, that the battle-lines could not have been drawn up more certainly through military art: this praise therefore, due to each of you in this bloodless battle, I bring [fero]: that neither could the argument have been proposed more subtly, nor avoided more acutely, in any way.
Asphal. Tu vero, Ereuni, luxuriaris, quasi non ipsa tua res ageretur. Probasne igitur semitam quam calcavit tibi Andabata, vel alia ingrederis?

Asphal. But you, Ereunius, run riot [luxuriaris], as if your own very affair [res] were not being conducted [ageretur]. Do you then approve the path which Andabata has trodden for you, or do you enter by another?
[Margin, p. 355: Tales propositiones non esse determinate veras aut falsas.]
[Margin, p. 355: That such propositions are not determinately true or false.]

Ereu. Ego vero eam summopere probo tanquam acutissimam & summo ingenio usque ad extrema perductam: quam tamen mihi ingredi non item fas puto. Homini ut nostis hebetiori, & qui nihil experimentis non obstetricantibus parturire valeam.

Ereu. I indeed approve it exceedingly, as most acute and carried through with the highest wit [ingenio] up to the extremes: which, however, I do not likewise think it lawful [fas] for me to enter — for a man, as you know, rather dull [hebetiori], and who am able to bring forth [parturire] nothing with experiments not acting as midwives [experimentis non obstetricantibus].

Considero enim num homines dum de futuris loquuntur, in ipsas res intendunt, an in causas. Videor autem mihi videre quod futura in semetipsis perspicere non possint, sicut praesentia sensu, praeterita memoria comprehendunt. Hic primum impingo.

For I consider whether men, while they speak about future [things], aim [intendunt] at the things themselves, or at the causes. And I seem to myself to see that they cannot perceive future [things] in themselves, as they comprehend present [things] by sense, past [things] by memory. Here I first strike [impingo].

Mox etiam medicum de morte vel vita aegri ut pronunciet, video pulsum & urinam inspicere; Nautam nubes & sydera & ventos, ut de tempestate praedicat, & similia in omni praevisione inspici. Unde certum mihi fit eos non loqui de futuritione, nisi prout in causis sunt.

Next also I see the physician, in order that he may pronounce about the death or life of the sick man, inspect the pulse and the urine; the Sailor, the clouds and stars and winds, in order that he may foretell [praedicat] about the weather [tempestate]; and that similar [things] are inspected in every foreseeing [praevisione]. Whence it becomes certain to me that they do not speak about futurition except according as [prout] [things] are in [their] causes.
Tandem hoc video innatum esse humano generi, ut nihil effutiat absque eo quod dicti rationem qualem qualem quantumvis ridiculam habeat, aut habere sibi videatur.

Lastly I see this to be inborn in the human race, that it blurts out [effutiat] nothing without having some reason [rationem] or other [qualem qualem] of what is said, however ridiculous, or seeming to itself to have [it].

Unde si experientia consulenda est, quae stultorum magistra est, certe mihi ea ingrediendum est qua Peripatetici & Thomistae semitam praeparaverunt: ut credam non esse determinate veras quae sunt de futuro contingenti propositiones, & suffosso, quo nitebatur aedificium tuum, fundamento, totam fabricam sic everto.

Whence, if experience is to be consulted, which is the mistress of fools, certainly I must enter by that [way] by which the Peripatetics and Thomists have prepared a path: so as to believe that the propositions which are about the contingent future are not determinately true; and, the foundation on which your edifice rested having been dug from under [suffosso], I thus overturn the whole structure [fabricam].

Andab. Sic evertis Asphalium, ut simul rationem & omnem scientiam; si enim contradictionis necessitas auferatur, quae ulterior est terra aut lapis angularis in qua pedem figamus, vel muros, ad scientiarum calles & turres superinducendos.

Andab. You so overturn Asphalius as [you overturn] at the same time reason and all science; for if the necessity of contradiction be taken away, what further earth is there, or corner-stone [lapis angularis], on which we may fix the foot, or the walls, for building over [superinducendos] the paths [calles] and towers of the sciences?
Ereu. Hoc ergo aeque nego, esse contradictorias has propositiones quae de futuris proferuntur.
Ereu. This then I equally deny, that these propositions which are put forth about future [things] are contradictories.
Andab. Quod tamen omnes Logici cum Aristotele ipso docent, & regulam figunt, cuilibet Enunciationi simplici, si praefigatur negatio, constitui contradictorias.

Andab. Which, however, all the Logicians with Aristotle himself teach, and they fix [it as] a rule, that to any simple Enunciation [Enunciationi], if a negation be prefixed, contradictories are constituted.

Ereu. Aliud est contradictoriarum nomine has propositiones appellare, aliud naturam contradictionis eis tribuere: hoc nego quemquam illorum facere qui indeterminatam earum veritatem propugnant: quantumvis in illud cum aliis consentiant.

Ereu. It is one thing to call these propositions by the name of contradictories, another to attribute to them the nature of contradiction: this I deny that any of those does who defend their indeterminate truth, however much they agree with the others in that [illud] [first thing].

Nam & hae propositiones: Aliquis homo est, aliquis non est, & hae Homo currit, Homo sedet & non sedet vel non currit & similes, voce tenus contradictoriae dici possunt, vim contradictoriarum habere non possunt.

For both these propositions, ‘Some man is’, ‘some [man] is not’, and these, ‘A man runs’, ‘A man sits’ and ‘does not sit’ or ‘does not run’, and similar ones, can be called contradictories as far as the word [voce tenus]; they cannot have the force of contradictories.

Andab. De similibus quidem non inficier quae asseris: clarum enim est aliud & aliud subiectum accipi in negatione & affirmatione. Hanc autem de futuris contingentibus sententiam commentus est Aristoteles, ut Stoicorum impetus declinaret absque alio fundamento.

Andab. About similar [propositions] indeed I shall not deny [inficier] what you assert: for it is clear that one and another subject is taken in the negation and the affirmation. But this opinion about contingent futures Aristotle devised [commentus est], in order to turn aside the onslaughts [impetus] of the Stoics, without any other foundation.

Ereu. Tu ergo quid putas? effectus contingentes suntne in causis suis determinate necne? v. c. pluvia in nube tam certone est, ut non possit a vento praeter optatum irruente dispelli nubes, vitari pluvia?

Ereu. What then do you think? Are contingent effects in their causes determinately or not? For example [v. c. = verbi causa]: is rain in the cloud so certainly, that the cloud cannot be dispersed by a wind rushing in beyond [what is] hoped, [and] the rain be avoided?
Andab. Non tam determinate sunt in causis.
Andab. They are not so determinately in the causes.

Ereu. Absolute ergo, effectus in tali causa existentia est indeterminata, & propositio de eo prolata ut in causa non potest esse determinate ei vel conformis vel difformis. Sicut paries albus parieti qui neque albus neque non a[l]bus foret, neque similis neque dissimilis foret.

Ereu. Absolutely, then, the existence of the effect in such a cause is indeterminate, and a proposition uttered about it as [it is] in the cause cannot be determinately either conformable or unconformable [difformis] to it. Just as a white wall would be neither similar nor dissimilar to a wall which would be neither white nor not white.
Andab. Verum paries talis neque imaginatione fingi potest & determinata propositio indeterminatae existentiae difformis est.
Andab. But such a wall cannot even be feigned by imagination; and a determinate proposition is unconformable [difformis] to an indeterminate existence.

Ereu. At propositio quae in mente est, abstrahere potest & esse indifferens, & eodem modo caussa effectum praecontinet dum adhuc aequaliter se habet ad quemlibet ex pluribus qui in ea latent. Quod nisi sic se habeat propositio falsa foret. At si eveniat effectum pro tempore esse conformem, vera erat: non enim de causa; sed de effectu in causa pronunciat assertio.

Ereu. But a proposition which is in the mind can abstract and be indifferent, and in the same way [as] a cause precontains [praecontinet] the effect while it is still equally disposed [se habet] to whichever of the several [effects] which lie hidden in it. Which unless the proposition be so disposed, it would be false. But if it comes about that the effect is, for the time [pro tempore], conformable, it was true: for the assertion pronounces not about the cause, but about the effect in the cause.

Et in hoc equidem non minimam huius difficultatis obscuritatem, sitam esse existimo, quod non advertant plerique, neque de effectu esse sermonem qui in sese determinatus est, neque aliter esse unquam potest: Neque de causa, de qua tantumdem est pronunciandum: sed de effectu prout est in causa, id est, secundum illum existendi modum quem in causa habet; hoc est in propensione defectibili quae valet, quod τὸ erit nisi quid impediat.

And in this indeed I judge not the least obscurity of this difficulty to be situated, that most do not advert that the discourse [sermonem] is neither about the effect which in itself is determinate, and cannot ever be otherwise; nor about the cause, about which just as much [tantumdem] must be pronounced; but about the effect according as it is in the cause, that is, according to that mode of existing which it has in the cause; that is, in a defectible propension [propensione defectibili], which is worth [valet] the same as [quod] ‘the will-be [τὸ erit] unless something hinder’.
Stat itaque esse effecti in tali causa non esse absolute esse, sed dumtaxat esse nisi quid impediat.
It stands, therefore, that the being of the effect in such a cause is not to be absolutely, but only to be unless something hinder.
Asphal. Ergo, qui omnes causas quae impedire possunt, viderit, poterit certo pronunciare, futurusne sit effectus necne?
Asphal. Therefore he who shall have seen all the causes which can hinder will be able to pronounce certainly whether the effect is future or not?
Ereu. Sic est.
Ereu. So it is.
Andab. Excipiendae sunt ab hac lege actiones voluntariae, quarum specialis est ratio.
Andab. Voluntary actions are to be excepted from this law, whose reason [ratio] is special.
Ereu. Tua causa hoc fiat, Andabata.
Ereu. For your sake [tua causa] let this be done, Andabata.
[Margin, p. 359: Fatum sane posse admitti.]
[Margin, p. 359: That fate can indeed be admitted.]
Asphal. Non itaque fatum evadis. Etsi enim non ex contradictionis vi, ex necessitate eveniant omnia; certe ex perpetua causarum serie non minus necessario omnia creabuntur.

Asphal. You do not therefore escape fate. For even if not from the force of contradiction all things come about from necessity, certainly from the perpetual series of causes all things will be created no less necessarily.

Ereu. Quando haec sic gererentur, ut dicis, si non fatum, certe nocens fatum declinatum erit. Fatum enim ut nostis, a fando dicitur; Deus autem fando cuncta procreavit, fando eadem continet & in suos quaeque effectus perducit.

Ereu. Though [quando] these [things] were so carried on, as you say, if not fate, certainly harmful fate will have been turned aside. For fate [fatum], as you know, is said from speaking [a fando]; but God by speaking [fando] procreated all things, by speaking holds the same together [continet] and leads each into its effects.

Dei autem notioni creata repugnare non posse aequum est, & perinde fato ipsius omnia iuxta evenire necessum est. Non itaque fatum horremus, si per fatum, seriem causarum a Deo directam & fortiter & suaviter a fine ad finem ab ipso praestitutum pertingentem intelligere velimus.

But it is fair [aequum] that created [things] cannot be repugnant [repugnare] to the notion [notioni] of God, and accordingly it is necessary [necessum est] that all things come about likewise [iuxta] by his fate. We do not therefore shudder at fate, if by fate we wish to understand the series of causes directed by God and reaching [pertingentem] both mightily and sweetly [fortiter & suaviter] from end to the end appointed [praestitutum] by him.
Asphal. Fateris itaque Dei consilium per causarum seriem, necessitatem causis & effectis fortuitis imponere.
Asphal. You confess, therefore, that the counsel [consilium] of God, through the series of causes, imposes necessity on fortuitous causes and effects.

Ereu. Neutiquam, sed dividenda est quaestio, & quid ad rem spectet & naturam, quid vero ad voces ex hominum usu derivatum, seponenda sunt: Hoc enim extra litem positum est, homines voces suis accommodare notionibus quas de rebus habent, non autem ipsis rebus, seu quod aliter dici solet, rebus prout in intellectu sunt, non autem prout in se sunt.

Ereu. By no means; but the question is to be divided, and what regards the thing [rem] and nature, and what [is] derived to the words [voces] from the usage of men, are to be set apart: for this is placed beyond dispute [extra litem], that men accommodate words to their notions which they have about things, but not to the things themselves; or, as is accustomed to be said otherwise, to things according as they are in the intellect, but not according as they are in themselves.

Sed neque cuiquam in mentem venire potest hominem quoties de futuro quicquam narrat, ad omnes causas etiam proximas rei advertere posse: tum quia actio in infinitis, id est, valde multis consistit, tum quia fortuita ea dicimus quae praevideri non possunt.

But neither can it come into anyone’s mind that a man, as often as he relates anything about the future, can advert to all the causes, even the proximate ones, of the thing: both because action consists in infinite [things], that is, very many, and because we call those [things] fortuitous which cannot be foreseen.

Respicit itaque homo ad causam per se, ex qua sequitur effectus quando sequitur, & ad pauca aliqua praeterea: & ex his pronunciat. Per haec autem non est definitus praefixe actionis exitus, sed incerte: Necessum proinde est ut effectus homini contingens & videatur & dicatur, necessitasque ab eo removenda.

Man therefore looks [respicit] to the cause through itself [per se], from which the effect follows when it follows, and to some few [things] besides; and from these he pronounces. But through these the outcome [exitus] of the action is not defined fixedly [praefixe], but uncertainly. It is necessary [necessum est] accordingly that the effect both seem and be called contingent to man, and that necessity [is] to be removed from it.
Si vero omnes causae consideratae forent, e diverso contingeret, omnem effectum necessitatem sapere, de contingentia nullum super fore sermonem.

But if all the causes were considered, it would happen on the contrary [e diverso] that every effect savours [sapere] of necessity, [and that] no discourse about contingency would be left over [super fore].

Haec modo colligamus. Ad rem pertinet, ut causae proximae sint contingentes & effecta, prout ex iis consequuntur. Ad rem rursus pertinet ut effecta ad omnes causas relata sint necessaria. Neque minus sit tota causarum collectio ad effectum aliquem comparata.

Let us now gather these [things]. It pertains to the thing [ad rem] that the proximate causes are contingent, and the effects, according as they follow from them. Again it pertains to the thing that effects, referred to all the causes, are necessary. Nor is the whole collection of causes, compared to any effect, less [so].

Ad voces pertinet ut quoniam communis hominum usus hoc habet, ut ad causam propriam & pauca alia respicientes absolute de rei natura pronuncient; Ex his autem incertus & contingens est effectus; Quoad voces autem proprietas ab eorum usu pendeat, vere effectus & earum causae contingentes dicantur.

It pertains to the words [ad voces] that — since the common usage of men has this, that looking to the proper cause and a few other [things] they pronounce absolutely about the nature of the thing; and from these the effect is uncertain and contingent; and [since], as regards words, propriety [proprietas] depends on their usage — effects and their causes are truly called contingent.

Item ut quoniam ad omnes causas respicere neque possint, neque soleant, necessarii effectus & causae absolute negentur esse. Non tamen sic, ut addito τῷ respectu omnium causarum, vel causae primae, non possint effecta necessaria appellari, vel etiam hae causae: cum necessaria causa non nisi indefectibilem in agendo sonet. Verum hoc cum addito, illud absolute dicitur, hoc secundum quid, illud simpliciter affirmatur.

Likewise, that, since they are neither able nor accustomed to look to all the causes, effects and causes are absolutely denied to be necessary. Not, however, so that, with ‘in respect [τῷ respectu] of all the causes’, or ‘of the first cause’, added, effects cannot be called necessary, or even these causes: since ‘necessary cause’ sounds [sonet] nothing but [a cause] indefectible in acting. But this is said with the addition, that absolutely; this is affirmed in a certain respect [secundum quid], that simply [simpliciter].

Andab. Iterum monendus es, Ereuni, ne quid ultra aras audeas. In praecipiti enim stas, & ni caveas, in illud rues ut Deum peccati causam facias: cum seriem causarum, necessitatem effectis inferre asseris.

Andab. Again you must be warned, Ereunius, lest you dare anything beyond the altars [ultra aras]. For you stand on a precipice, and unless you beware, you will rush into this, that you make God the cause of sin: when you assert that the series of causes brings [inferre] necessity upon the effects.
Ereu. Moneri patiar & a te, Andabata, sed non in hac causa, postquam in tui gratiam actus humanos ex tota hac disputatione seclusimus.
Ereu. I will suffer to be warned even by you, Andabata, but not in this case [causa], since [postquam] for your sake [in tui gratiam] we have shut out human acts from this whole disputation.

terms: Printed with œ (cœpisti, ‘you have begun’); taken as the common 17th-century spelling of cepisti (capio).
Andabata picks up Asphalius’ ‘ita ut non sim captus’ (‘so that I am not caught’) just before: the dialectical trap has now closed on Andabata himself.

Thomist-Bañezian vocabulary of God’s prior decree of free acts; the ‘moderns’ (Molinists) adopted the account of futurition through the truth of propositions precisely to avoid making God’s decree the origin of free acts.
In 1640s scholastic usage, the recent (chiefly Jesuit/Molinist) theologians, as against the ancient Thomists.
The objects of Molina’s scientia media (what a free creature would do if placed in given circumstances), said here to be ‘necessary for regulating human liberty’ in the divine cognition.
without his own share of the danger
Also ‘without any part of the danger to himself’.

Quoted as verse (‘ut ille canit’), a hexameter close; the poet is not identified with certainty. White’s anecdote of Massinissa as a mere spectator of Zama is his own; Massinissa in fact fought there with his cavalry.
Livy 30.35 and Polybius 15.15–16: after Zama Scipio and others praised Hannibal’s disposition of his battle-line; White makes the praise mutual.
Proverbial (cf. Livy 22.39 ‘eventus stultorum magister’); Ereunius ironically owns himself one who learns only from experiments.
with experiments not acting as midwives
Socratic maieutic image turned empiricist: Ereunius (the ‘searcher’) can bring forth nothing without experimental evidence.
The reading of Aristotle, De interpretatione 9, that singular future-contingent propositions are not determinately true or false; Aquinas, In Peri herm. I lect. 13–15.
Biblical (Ps. 117/118:22; Eph. 2:20): the principle of contradiction as the foundation of science.
Printed clearly ‘calles’; paired oddly with ‘towers’ and ‘walls’, kept literally.
Boethian term for Aristotle’s apophansis; the logicians’ rule that prefixing a negation to any simple enunciation yields its contradictory.
Indefinite propositions such as ‘Homo currit / Homo non currit’ can both be true (different subjects taken), hence are not true contradictories; Ereunius assimilates future-contingent pairs to these.
Truth as conformity of proposition to being (cf. conformitas / deformitas, D3-N10 p1).
Scholastic: the effect pre-exists virtually in its cause (cf. praehaberi, D3-N09).
White’s analysis of contingent being-in-the-cause: the effect is there as ‘what will be unless something hinders’ — the Aristotelian ‘for the most part’.
The Greek article used to nominalise a phrase, as in scholastic Latin (cf. τὸ dum, D3-N10 p1).
The proposition becomes true when the effect actually comes to be conformable.
Varro, De lingua Latina 6.52; Augustine, De civitate Dei 5.9; White Christianises it: God made, sustains and governs all things ‘by speaking’ (fando; cf. Gen. 1, Ps. 32/33:9).
fortiter & suaviter a fine ad finem
mightily and sweetly from end to end
Wisdom 8:1 (Vulgate: ‘attingit … a fine usque ad finem fortiter et disponit omnia suaviter’), the classic text for providence through secondary causes.
Aristotelian per se vs per accidens causality: men predict from the essential cause and a few others, not from the whole concourse.
The scholastic distinction (Aristotle, Soph. el. 5): effects are necessary only with the addition ‘in respect of all causes’.
Proverb ‘amicus usque ad aras’ (Gellius 1.3.20, Pericles): go along with a friend only as far as religion allows — here, not so far as to make God the cause of sin.
Asphalius rebukes Ereunius’ florid praise when his own thesis is at stake.
notes: Unit: Dialogue III, Knot x, part 2 of 2 (end of Knot x). PDF pp. 364–372 = printed pp. 353–361, from Andabata’s ‘Verum tu me prorsus coepisti’ (p. 353, margin ‘Veritatem propositionum de futuro contingenti non salvare libertatem’, continued on p. 354) to Ereunius’ ‘…ex tota hac disputatione seclusimus.’ (p. 361). Offset +11 holds (running heads 353–362). Signatures Yy (p. 353), Yy ij (p. 355), Yy iij (p. 357), Zz (p. 361). Boundary with Knot xi: the margin ‘Nodus XI. Deum nullius mali esse causam’ stands at the top of p. 362 inside Ereunius’ speech that began on p. 361 (‘Moneri patiar…’). The knot is taken to begin at ‘Verum me tam alienum ab hoc errore habe, ut nihil mali a prima causa ortum habere suspicari possim’ (p. 361), which states the knot’s thesis, following the precedent of D2-N14 (a knot beginning within a speech); the preceding sentence, which closes the exchange about fate, is kept here.

Uncertain readings and constructions: (1) p. 353 ‘coepisti’ (printed cœpisti) — read as cepisti, ‘you have caught’. (2) p. 354 margin ‘non salvare libertatem’ — accusative + infinitive with ‘Veritatem’ (printed ‘Veritatē’), ‘that the truth … does not save liberty’. (3) p. 354 ‘quam viam ingrediendum sit’ — impersonal gerundive with an accusative object; kept literally. (4) p. 354 ‘(ut ille canit) sua sine parte pericli’ — the poet is not identified; translated as a quotation. (5) p. 355 ‘ut de tempestate praedicat’ — indicative after ut where the subjunctive praedicet is expected (parallel to ‘ut pronunciet’); taken as purpose. (6) p. 356 ‘calles’ — clear in print; possibly for colles. In the same sentence ‘vel muros, ad scientiarum calles & turres superinducendos’ the gerundive is taken with calles & turres (‘for building over the paths and towers’); it could instead agree with muros (‘or the walls to be built over, for the paths and towers of the sciences’). (7) p. 357 ‘neque non abus’ — misprint for albus, printed [l]. (8) p. 358 ‘& eodem modo caussa effectum praecontinet’ — read as a comparison (‘in the same way [as] a cause precontains’); it could also be a separate coordinated statement (‘and in the same way the cause precontains the effect’). (9) p. 359 ‘Quando haec sic gererentur’ — quando with the imperfect subjunctive, taken as concessive (‘though’). (10) p. 360 ‘Neque minus sit tota causarum collectio…’ — subjunctive ‘sit’ in a list of indicative/ut-clauses, taken as depending loosely on ‘Ad rem pertinet ut’; English supplies ‘[so]’. (11) p. 360–361 the long sentence ‘Ad voces pertinet ut quoniam … dicantur’ is anacoluthic; the English keeps the order with dashes. No illegible readings.

The transcription check found no discrepancies. The translation check produced 3 corrections: (i) p. 357 ‘Stoicorum impetus’ — first drafted as singular ‘the onslaught’; impetus taken as accusative plural, ‘the onslaughts [impetus]’; (ii)–(iii) pp. 360–361 respicere ad (‘Respicit itaque homo ad causam’, ‘ad causam propriam … respicientes’, ‘ad omnes causas respicere’) — first drafted ‘look back to’, a too-etymological rendering; set to ‘look to’ (have regard to) in all three places for consistency.
